chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: 'The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [with] corruption is that they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be exchanged or that they be exiled from the land,' [to the end of the verse]. I said: Which of these penalties specified by Allah are upon them? He said: That is up to the Imam; if he wills, he will behead, if he wills, he will crucify, if he wills, he will exile, if he wills, he will kill. I said: Exile to where? He said: He is exiled from one province to another province. And he said: Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) exiled two men from Kufa to Basra. So the explanation in this report is one of two things: One is that we carry it on taqiyya (dissimulation), because among the general public (Sunni scholars) is one who says that the Imam is free to choose among these penalties, and does not restrict them to what the first narration and the reports we mentioned in our Great Book contained.
ai.seo_question: What are the discretionary penalties for hudat al-qatl in Shia jurisprudence according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies that the four penalties in Surah Al-Ma'idah (5:33) are not mutually exclusive but represent a discretionary range (ikhtiyar) for the Imam, who may choose execution, crucifixion, exile, or amputation based on the severity of the crime. The text highlights the scholarly debate regarding whether this flexibility contradicts stricter interpretations, ultimately attributing the broader scope to the Imam's authority and noting the historical precedent of Ali ibn Abi Talib exiling criminals from Kufa to Basra. This establishes the principle of judicial discretion in Shia fiqh, distinguishing it from the more rigid application often found in Sunni jurisprudence.
